recent_posts.title: The duality of language models in the browser
recent_posts.summary: Dave Rupert shares a nuanced take on small language models (SLMs) running natively in the browser via Chrome and Edge's experimental Prompt, Summarizer, and Rewriter APIs. He outlines genuine appeal: local/private execution, no API keys, no per-token costs, lower energy use, and a low barrier to prototyping. However, he also endorses Mozilla's concerns about model calcification (sites tuning prompts to Google's specific model, echoing the Chrome-only era), model neutrality (Google's TOS becoming the de-facto standard), and the false promise of universal access when GPU-equipped devices are required. He proposes alternatives including a bring-your-own-model marketplace, stronger fallback stories for low-end devices, and spec-level guidance on prohibited use cases — or abandoning the spec entirely if accuracy problems can't be solved.

recent_posts.title: AI code generation creates cognitive debt that burns out developers
recent_posts.summary: AI coding tools are causing burnout among their most enthusiastic users by overwhelming the human brain's limited capacity to manage the output. Drawing on Goldratt's 'The Goal', the argument is that AI-generated code creates excess inventory — more files, more context, more cognitive debt — without fixing the real bottleneck: human understanding. Over-generating code leads to abandoned projects, security/accessibility blind spots, and compounding context-switching costs. The 40-watt human brain, not the GPU, is the true constraint, and developers should be cautious about producing more than they can meaningfully comprehend.

recent_posts.title: People are not friction
recent_posts.summary: A critical perspective on the AI-as-frictionless-automation narrative, arguing that treating people as friction is dangerous. Drawing on the Gell-Mann Amnesia Effect, the author warns that LLMs produce dopamine-inducing but unreliable outputs, amplify both good and bad patterns, and lack genuine understanding. The post pushes back against the idea that AI can replace designers, engineers, or any human collaborator, emphasizing that people carry contextual knowledge and nuance that machines cannot replicate.

recent_posts.title: AI skills are magic words with unpredictable results
recent_posts.summary: AI 'skills' — text files optionally injected into an agent's context window — are compared to magic numbers in programming: workarounds with unpredictable results and no reliable way to measure effectiveness. The non-deterministic nature of LLMs means the same skill can produce wildly different outputs, making quality consistency difficult. Questions around minimum viable context, token costs, and context rot remain unanswered. The author expresses skepticism about the broader churn of AI tooling trends (skills, MCP, PRDs, prompt engineering) and anticipates greater scrutiny once AI subsidies end and users bear the full cost of hallucinations.

recent_posts.title: Why I stopped building side projects that depend on third-party APIs
recent_posts.summary: A developer reflects on repeatedly hitting dead ends when trying to build side project prototypes due to lack of public API access — from tennis rankings to real estate listings. Frustrated by the decline of freely accessible APIs since the Web 2.0 era, the author decides to swear off API-dependent ideas entirely as a personal filter. The post also touches on the risks of building on third-party platforms (OAuth apps, Tweetbot-style shutdowns) and the CarPlay template restrictions discovered along the way.

recent_posts.title: How I redesigned my personal site with monospace fonts named grid lines and view transitions
recent_posts.summary: Dave Rupert shares the details of his 2026 personal site redesign, highlighting three main changes: switching to Cascadia Mono as a monospace font sitewide, adopting named CSS grid lines for flexible layout control, and expanding multi-page view transitions. He also reduced his CSS by 40% (~150 lines, ~0.8 KB compressed) by leveraging modern CSS features like nesting, :is(), :has(), and :where(). The post covers what stayed the same, the reasoning behind each decision, and how named grid lines open up future art direction possibilities.

recent_posts.title: Focus rings with nested contrast-color()?
recent_posts.summary: An exploration of using nested `contrast-color()` CSS functions to automatically generate accessible focus ring styles from a single background color token. The technique uses `contrast-color(contrast-color(var(--page-bg)))` to derive both the outer ring and inner highlight colors. The post also weighs this against using `color-scheme` with `light-dark()` as a simpler, better-supported alternative for theming focus rings across light and dark modes, ultimately recommending the latter for its readability and broader browser support.

recent_posts.title: Interpolate contrast-color() to manipulate lightness
recent_posts.summary: A technique for using CSS contrast-color() to manipulate button hover states by adjusting lightness rather than mixing black or white. By interpolating contrast-color() into a numeric value (1 or -1) via CSS if() statements and @property, you can use oklch() relative color syntax to lighten or darken a color along its natural lightness ramp. This produces warmer, more harmonious hover states compared to color-mix() with black/white, and offers finer control over the step amount and even chroma adjustments.

recent_posts.title: Using your design system colors with contrast-color()
recent_posts.summary: The CSS contrast-color() function only returns black or white, which is limiting for design systems that need brand-specific colors. Using Lea Verou's --contrast-color() workaround alongside the upcoming CSS if() function, you can map contrast results to your own design tokens. The technique requires registering a custom property with @property to enable color-type comparisons in style queries, then using an if() statement to select the appropriate design system token based on whether the contrast result is light or dark.

recent_posts.title: Algorithmic hover states with contrast-color()
recent_posts.summary: Firefox 146 added support for the CSS `contrast-color()` function, joining Safari 26. The function takes a color input and returns either white or black based on maximum contrast. Beyond foreground text color, it can be used to algorithmically determine hover/focus state background colors — mixing in white or black depending on the button's current background. Combined with `color-mix()` and a polyfill using CSS `@function` for Chromium 139+, this enables fully algorithmic, accessible button states without extra tokens or theme-specific overrides. The technique is especially valuable for design systems where button background colors are user-controlled.
